name: Ghum
tagline: India's highest railway station, Batasia Loop and an old monastery
meta_description: Ghum near Darjeeling: Batasia Loop, the DHR museum at India's highest station, Yiga Choeling monastery and steam joyrides. Costs, timings and tips.
summary: Ghum is a small, often foggy town at 2,258 m, about 7 km from Darjeeling, on the saddle where the toy train tops out. It has India's highest railway station and its museum, Batasia Loop with the Gorkha War Memorial, and Yiga Choeling, the old Ghum monastery founded in 1850. See it in half a day from Darjeeling.
intro: Ghum sits on the pass between the Darjeeling ridge and the road down to Kurseong and Siliguri. Every vehicle and every train going to Darjeeling crosses it, and many visitors see nothing but a foggy bazaar through the window. Stop, though, and Ghum gives you three of the best sights in the district within a couple of kilometres: the station, the loop and the monastery.

Ghum station, at 2,258 m, is the highest on India's railways. The Darjeeling Himalayan Railway keeps a small museum in the old station building, and steam and diesel joyrides from Darjeeling stop here for half an hour so you can see it. Below the station, the line spirals over itself at Batasia Loop, with a memorial to Gorkha soldiers and, on clear days, Kangchenjunga behind.

Up a lane from the bazaar is Yiga Choeling, the old Ghum monastery, with a tall seated Maitreya, the future Buddha, inside a hall lit by butter lamps. Ghum is cooler and mistier than Darjeeling, and at night it can be close to freezing in winter. Most people visit on the way back from Tiger Hill at dawn, or on a toy-train joyride. Budget half a day and wear a warm layer.

story.title: The top of the line
paras: When Franklin Prestage's engineers pushed the Darjeeling Himalayan Railway up from the plains between 1879 and 1881, they had to lift a train from about 100 m at Siliguri to over 2,200 m at Ghum on a 2-foot gauge. They did it with tight curves, loops and zig-zag reverses, where the train runs forward, stops, and backs up a second line to gain height. Ghum was the summit; from here the line drops into Darjeeling.

The drop was too steep for comfort, so in 1919 the railway built Batasia Loop, a spiral where the track circles a hill and crosses over itself, easing the descent. The name is commonly explained from the Nepali 'batas', wind, because the spot is so exposed. In 1999 UNESCO listed the railway as a World Heritage Site, and Ghum station, with its museum, became the place to tell its story.
story.source: UNESCO World Heritage listing, Mountain Railways of India (1999); Darjeeling Himalayan Railway museum, Ghum

did_you_know: Ghum station, at 2,258 m, is the highest railway station in India.
Batasia Loop was completed in 1919 to ease the steep descent from Ghum to Darjeeling.
Yiga Choeling, the old Ghum monastery, was founded in 1850 by Lama Sherab Gyatso and follows the Gelug school.
facts: Highest railway station, Batasia Loop, Yiga Choeling

highlights.title: Batasia Loop
highlights.text: The toy train spirals over itself round a garden on a hill, with the Gorkha War Memorial at the centre. On clear mornings Kangchenjunga stands behind the memorial and Darjeeling town spreads along the ridge. Entry is about ₹20–50, indicative 2026.

highlights.title: India's highest station
highlights.text: Ghum station, at 2,258 m, tops India's railway network. The old station building holds a small museum of engine parts, tickets, lamps and photographs from the line's first century.

highlights.title: Yiga Choeling monastery
highlights.text: Founded in 1850, the old Ghum monastery holds a tall seated image of Maitreya, the Buddha to come, surrounded by butter lamps, old texts and murals. It is a short walk up a lane from the bazaar.

highlights.title: Steam joyride from Darjeeling
highlights.text: The DHR's two-hour joyrides from Darjeeling stop at Batasia Loop and spend about half an hour at Ghum for the museum. Steam runs cost about ₹1,500–1,600 and diesel about ₹800–1,000, indicative 2026.

highlights.title: The Tiger Hill return
highlights.text: Most Tiger Hill sunrise cars stop at Ghum monastery and Batasia Loop on the way back to Darjeeling. Ask your driver to include both, so you see Ghum before the day's crowds.

how_to_reach.text: Any shared jeep from Darjeeling's Chowk Bazaar stand heading to Siliguri, Kurseong, Mirik or Sukhiapokhri passes through Ghum. Ask to be dropped at Ghum bazaar: ₹30–60 a seat, 20–30 minutes, indicative 2026.

Most visitors see Ghum on the Tiger Hill sunrise trip, with stops at Ghum monastery and Batasia Loop: ₹1,500–2,200 per car, indicative 2026. A short taxi from Darjeeling to Ghum and back costs about ₹600–1,000.

The toy train is the classic way: joyrides from Darjeeling to Ghum and back take about two hours, and the daily NJP–Darjeeling train passes through. Bagdogra (IXB) is about 65 km away. Book trains on IRCTC and check current status before you travel.

where_to_stay: Ghum is best seen in half a day from Darjeeling, about 7 km away, where the choice of hotels is much wider: WBTDC's Darjeeling Tourism Property and Revolver for budget, Dekeling and the Bellevue for comfort, and the Windamere or Mayfair Hill Resort for heritage. A few simple lodges and homestays exist around Ghum and on the road to Lepchajagat, but Ghum is often in fog and is colder than Darjeeling, so most travellers are happier sleeping in town and coming out for the morning.
costs: Small fee, or included in joyride
budget_tip: Take the diesel joyride instead of steam if you just want the route: it stops at the same places, Batasia and the Ghum museum, for about ₹600 less per person.
tips: Ghum is often in fog after 10 am; go early for any chance of a clear view at Batasia.
Carry a warm layer and a hat even in May; Ghum is 2–3 °C colder than Darjeeling and windy.
Walk up the lane to Yiga Choeling rather than driving; it is a few minutes and the bazaar is worth seeing.
Do not cross the tracks at Batasia while a train is due; staff will tell you when to stand clear.
Joyride seats sell out in October and May; book on IRCTC as soon as your dates are fixed.

experiences.title: Batasia Loop at first light
experiences.summary: Batasia Loop, built in 1919, is where the toy train spirals around a hill and crosses over its own track below Ghum. The garden inside holds the Gorkha War Memorial, and on clear mornings Kangchenjunga rises behind it.
body: Batasia Loop lies about 5 km from Darjeeling, just below Ghum. The line circles a small hill in a full spiral and passes over itself, a solution the railway adopted in 1919 to ease the steep fall from Ghum. The garden inside the loop is laid out with paths and flower beds and is well kept by the railway.

At the centre stands the Gorkha War Memorial, raised to honour Gorkha soldiers of the Indian Army who died in the country's service. A bronze soldier stands on a stepped base, with names and inscriptions around it. Many visitors from the hills come here to pay respects, so be quiet near the memorial.

Come at first light, ideally on the way back from Tiger Hill. On clear mornings from October to April, Kangchenjunga rises behind the memorial and Darjeeling's ridge spreads to the right. Wait for a train if you can: watching it curve round and climb the loop is the best part. Stalls by the gate sell woollens, tea and snacks.

faqs.q: What is the entry fee for Batasia Loop
faqs.a: About ₹20–50 per person, indicative 2026, paid at the gate. Joyride passengers enter during the train's stop. The garden opens early, usually around sunrise, so you can visit after Tiger Hill. Check current status before you travel, as fees change.

faqs.q: Why was Batasia Loop built
faqs.a: The drop from Ghum, the line's summit, into Darjeeling was too steep, so in 1919 the railway built a spiral loop where the track circles a hill and passes over itself. This lengthens the route and eases the gradient. It is now one of the most photographed spots on the line.

faqs.q: What is the Gorkha War Memorial at Batasia
faqs.a: It is a memorial inside Batasia Loop to Gorkha soldiers of the Indian Army who died in service. A bronze statue of a soldier stands on a stepped base. Treat it as a place of remembrance: keep your voice down and do not climb on the base for photos.

experiences.title: Yiga Choeling, the old Ghum monastery
experiences.best_time: Mornings, all year; Losar in Feb–Mar
experiences.summary: Founded in 1850 by Lama Sherab Gyatso, Yiga Choeling is the best-known monastery in the Darjeeling hills. Its hall holds a tall seated Maitreya, the Buddha to come, with butter lamps, old texts and painted walls.
body: Yiga Choeling, often called the old Ghum monastery, was founded in 1850 by Lama Sherab Gyatso and belongs to the Gelug school of Tibetan Buddhism, the school of the Dalai Lama. It stands up a short lane from Ghum bazaar, a two-storey building with a courtyard, prayer wheels and a view down the valley.

Inside the main hall sits an image of Maitreya, the future Buddha, about 4.5 metres tall, seated rather than cross-legged, as is the custom for Maitreya. Butter lamps burn in front, and the walls hold murals and shelves of old texts. Monks chant here morning and evening.

Visitors are welcome. Walk clockwise round the building and spin the prayer wheels as you go. Remove shoes before entering, and ask before taking photographs; inside the hall it is usually not allowed. A small donation in the box is the custom. The Samten Choeling monastery, another Gelug house, is a short walk away.

faqs.q: When was Ghum Monastery built
faqs.a: Yiga Choeling, the old Ghum monastery, was founded in 1850 by Lama Sherab Gyatso. It follows the Gelug school of Tibetan Buddhism. The present building has been repaired and added to since, but it remains one of the oldest monasteries in the Darjeeling hills.

faqs.q: Is photography allowed in Ghum Monastery
faqs.a: Usually not inside the main prayer hall, though rules vary; ask the monk on duty. Photographs of the courtyard and outside are generally fine. Never use a flash near the images, and do not photograph monks at prayer without asking.

faqs.q: How do I get to Ghum Monastery from Darjeeling
faqs.a: Take any shared jeep heading to Ghum, Kurseong or Siliguri for ₹30–60, indicative 2026, and get off at Ghum bazaar, then walk up the lane in a few minutes. Most Tiger Hill sunrise cars stop here on the way back to Darjeeling.

experiences.title: The railway museum at Ghum station
experiences.cost: Small fee, or included in joyride ticket
experiences.image_query: Ghum station museum Darjeeling Himalayan Railway
experiences.summary: The old building at Ghum station, India's highest at 2,258 m, now holds the Darjeeling Himalayan Railway's museum: engine parts, lamps, tickets, signal gear and photographs from the line's long history, with an old steam engine outside.
body: Ghum station marks the summit of the Darjeeling Himalayan Railway. From here the line drops north into Darjeeling and south through Sonada and Kurseong to the plains. The station building houses a museum laid out over a few rooms, showing how a 2-foot gauge railway was built and run in the mountains from 1881.

Displays include old tickets and ticket presses, lamps, uniforms, signalling equipment, engine parts and photographs of construction, landslides and royal visitors. Captions explain the loops and reverses that let trains climb so steeply. Outside on the platform, an old steam engine is kept on display.

Joyride passengers from Darjeeling get about half an hour here, enough for the museum and a cup of tea. If you come by road, ask at the station for entry; there is usually a small fee. Ghum is often foggy, so the museum makes a good stop whatever the weather. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is the Ghum railway museum included in the joyride
faqs.a: Yes. DHR joyrides between Darjeeling and Ghum stop at Ghum station for about 30 minutes so passengers can visit the museum, and the joyride also stops at Batasia Loop. Arrangements change, so confirm when you book on IRCTC.

faqs.q: Can I visit the Ghum museum without taking the train
faqs.a: Yes. Ghum is about 7 km from Darjeeling by road. Walk into the station and ask for museum entry; there is usually a small fee. Opening hours follow the station's working day, so go in the morning.

faqs.q: Why is Ghum the highest railway station in India
faqs.a: At 2,258 m, Ghum is the summit of the Darjeeling Himalayan Railway, which climbs from about 100 m at Siliguri. No other station on India's railway network sits higher, which is why it is a popular stop on every joyride.

experiences.title: Steam joyride from Darjeeling to Ghum
experiences.image_query: Darjeeling toy train steam engine B class
experiences.summary: A two-hour return ride from Darjeeling to Ghum behind a B-class steam engine, the type that has hauled the toy train for well over a century. The train stops at Batasia Loop and spends half an hour at Ghum's museum.
body: The B-class engines are small 0-4-0 saddle-tank locomotives built for the Darjeeling line from 1889 by British makers such as Sharp Stewart and the North British Locomotive Company. A few still work, coaxed up the grade with coal and water, and they are the stars of the joyrides. Hearing one work hard up to Ghum is the reason to choose steam.

Joyrides leave Darjeeling station several times a day in season. The train climbs about 7 km to Ghum, stops at Batasia Loop for photographs, then waits about half an hour at Ghum for the museum before returning. A full trip takes around two hours. Seats are in small coaches, so book early.

Steam costs about ₹1,500–1,600 and diesel about ₹800–1,000, indicative 2026. Festive specials have been announced for October 2026 to January 2027. Book on IRCTC up to the advance reservation limit, as October and May sell out. Services change with weather and engine availability, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How much is the Darjeeling toy train joyride
faqs.a: About ₹1,500–1,600 for a steam joyride and ₹800–1,000 for diesel, indicative 2026, for a two-hour return trip to Ghum with stops at Batasia Loop and the Ghum museum. Special festive services may cost differently. Book on IRCTC and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is the steam joyride better than diesel
faqs.a: For the experience, yes: the B-class steam engines are over a century old in design, and the sound and smoke are the heart of the toy train. The route and stops are the same on diesel, which is cheaper and more likely to have seats. Choose steam if it fits your budget.

faqs.q: How do I book the Darjeeling toy train joyride
faqs.a: Book on IRCTC's website or app, choosing Darjeeling as both start and end station and the joyride service you want, or at the booking counter at Darjeeling station if seats remain. Book early for October and May. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How far is Ghum from Darjeeling
faqs.a: About 7 km, 20–30 minutes by road or roughly an hour by toy train with the Batasia stop. Shared jeeps heading to Kurseong, Siliguri or Mirik pass through Ghum for ₹30–60, indicative 2026.

faqs.q: Is Ghum the highest railway station in India
faqs.a: Yes. Ghum station on the Darjeeling Himalayan Railway stands at 2,258 m, the highest on India's railway network. Its old building houses a small museum about the railway.

faqs.q: What is there to see in Ghum
faqs.a: Batasia Loop with the Gorkha War Memorial, the DHR museum at Ghum station, Yiga Choeling monastery founded in 1850, and Samten Choeling monastery nearby. All four fit into half a day, usually combined with Tiger Hill at dawn.

faqs.q: Should I stay in Ghum or Darjeeling
faqs.a: Stay in Darjeeling. Ghum is only 7 km away, much smaller, often foggy and colder. Darjeeling has far more hotels at every budget, plus restaurants and transport. Visit Ghum in the morning on the Tiger Hill trip or a joyride.

faqs.q: Why is Ghum always foggy
faqs.a: Ghum sits on a saddle at 2,258 m where moist air from the plains rises and cools, so cloud forms here often, especially from June to September and later in the day. Mornings from October to April give the best chance of clear views.

faqs.q: Is Batasia Loop worth visiting
faqs.a: Yes, for its mountain view, the Gorkha War Memorial and the chance to see the toy train circle the loop. It takes 30–45 minutes, costs ₹20–50, and is usually included on the Tiger Hill return trip or joyride.

faqs.q: Can I walk from Darjeeling to Ghum
faqs.a: Yes. It is about 7 km along Hill Cart Road beside the railway, mostly uphill from Darjeeling. Allow 1.5–2 hours. The road is busy with jeeps, so walk on the railway side with care and keep clear of trains. Take a shared jeep back.

faqs.q: How cold is Ghum
faqs.a: Colder than Darjeeling by 2–3 °C. Winter days are around 3–9 °C with nights near or below freezing, and summer days 12–17 °C. Fog and wind make it feel colder. Bring a jacket, gloves and a hat for early starts.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Ghum
faqs.a: October to December and March to April for clear mornings and mountain views. Go early in the day; fog often closes in by late morning. June to September is the wettest and foggiest time, though the museum and monastery are worth seeing in any weather.
